_about: The weekly mysteries (game/core/weekly_mystery.gd): five clues, one opening each weekday, one guess.

mysteries.title: The monsoon fever
mysteries.patient: Mr. Santosh Kadam, 34, office peon, Kurla
clues: Fever, headache and a body ache 'like a truck went over me', five days now. Paracetamol from the chemist, twice.
His calves hurt so much he can't climb the stairs at the station. He says it's the calves, specifically. He's very specific.
Last Tuesday the trains stopped and he waded home through knee-deep flood water. 'Everyone did, Doctor. What to do?'
His eyes are red, but there's no discharge and nothing itches. His urine has gone dark and there's not much of it. Creatinine 3.1.
Today he's yellow. Platelets 62,000, bilirubin 6. The rat poison shop near his chawl is doing very good business.
mysteries.explain: Flood water, rats, terrible calf pain, red eyes without discharge, then kidneys and jaundice: leptospirosis. Every Mumbai monsoon. Doxycycline or penicillin, and dialysis if the kidneys stop.

mysteries.title: The farmer who kept coming back
clues: Fever for eight days, high, with chills. Malaria test negative twice. Typhoid test 'weakly positive', which means nothing.
Bad headache, a dry cough, and his eyes are a bit red. Two courses of antibiotics from the village clinic did nothing.
Lymph nodes swollen in the armpit. Liver enzymes up, platelets 90,000.
Before the fever, he spent a week clearing scrub and long grass on the bund behind his field.
Under his left arm, where nobody looked: a painless black scab with a red ring round it, like a cigarette burn.
mysteries.explain: Fever that ignores ordinary antibiotics, bush clearing, and an eschar hiding in the armpit: scrub typhus, from a mite bite. Doxycycline works in a day or two. Always look in the armpits and the groin.

mysteries.title: The battery man's stomach
clues: Belly cramps on and off for two months, bad enough to bend him double. Two scans: nothing. 'Gas,' said the last doctor.
Constipated, tired, and his haemoglobin is 9. Iron tablets for a month have changed nothing.
His right wrist has gone weak; he can't lift his hand back. He keeps dropping his chai glass.
He works in a small battery recycling unit. No gloves, no mask, and lunch on the workbench.
A thin blue-grey line along his gums. The blood film shows red cells with little dots in them (basophilic stippling).
mysteries.explain: Colicky belly pain, anaemia that iron doesn't fix, wrist drop, a gum line and stippled red cells, in a battery recycler: lead. Blood lead level, out of the exposure, and chelation if it's high.

mysteries.title: The tingling feet
clues: Her feet tingle and burn, worse at night. She's been told it's 'just age'. She disagrees, strongly.
She's tired all the time, a bit breathless on the stairs, and pale. Her tongue is red, smooth and sore.
Strictly vegetarian all her life, no eggs. Diabetic for twelve years, on metformin the whole time.
Haemoglobin 9.2, but the red cells are big: MCV 112. Iron studies normal.
She's become forgetful, and in the dark she sways when she closes her eyes. Her daughter thought it was the start of dementia.
mysteries.explain: Big red cells, a sore tongue, tingling, unsteadiness in the dark and forgetfulness, in a lifelong vegetarian on metformin: B12 deficiency. Injections fix it, if it's caught before the nerves give up.

mysteries.title: Tired, cold and gaining
clues: Exhausted for six months. She sleeps nine hours and wakes up tired. Her husband says she's 'just lazy now'.
Five kilos up without eating more. Constipated. She wears a sweater in May, in Nagpur.
Her skin is dry, her hair is falling out, and her periods have become heavy.
Her voice is hoarse, her face looks puffy in the mornings, and her pulse is 54.
Her ankle reflexes come back slowly, like they're thinking about it. Cholesterol has gone up too.
mysteries.explain: Tired, cold, weight up, constipated, dry skin, heavy periods, a slow pulse and slow reflexes: an underactive thyroid. A TSH test and a tablet a day. Somebody should also have a word with the husband.

mysteries.title: The back that wouldn't get better
clues: Back pain for three months, in the middle of the back. Physiotherapy and painkillers: no change.
The pain wakes him at night. He's lost six kilos and doesn't feel like eating.
A low fever every evening, and sweats that soak the sheet. His roommate had a cough 'for a long time' last year.
Pressing on one bone in the middle of his back makes him jump. A small bump is starting to stick out there.
The X-ray shows two vertebrae collapsing into each other, and the disc between them is gone.
mysteries.explain: Months of back pain with night pain, weight loss, evening fevers and sweats, a contact with a cough, and two vertebrae eaten away with the disc: TB of the spine (Pott's). Six months or more of TB treatment, free under the national programme.

mysteries.title: The boy who stopped growing
clues: Short for his age, and smaller than his younger cousin. His mother says he 'eats like a horse'.
Loose, pale, smelly stools, and a big belly on thin arms and legs.
Anaemic. A year of iron syrup hasn't helped at all.
It all started at about one year old, around when his grandmother began giving him chapatis.
A blood test for tissue transglutaminase antibodies comes back strongly positive.
mysteries.explain: Poor growth, pale fatty stools, a big belly, anaemia that iron can't fix, all starting with wheat: coeliac disease. Common in North India. No wheat, ever, and he catches up.

mysteries.title: The anaemia that iron didn't fix
clues: Her haemoglobin is 10.4. The college doctor started iron tablets. A year later: 10.5.
She feels fine. She's never had heavy periods, and she eats well (her hostel mess disagrees).
The red cells are very small: MCV 63. But her red cell count is high, 6.1 million.
Her ferritin is normal. So is her serum iron.
HbA2 on electrophoresis: 5.6%. Her parents are first cousins, and her mother 'has also been anaemic forever'.
mysteries.explain: Very small cells with a high red cell count, normal iron and a raised HbA2: beta thalassaemia trait. Stop the iron. And test the partner before marriage, because two traits can make a child with thalassaemia major.

mysteries.title: The fever that comes and goes
mysteries.patient: Mr. Ramesh Gowda, 44, dairy farmer, Mandya
clues: Fever for six weeks. Not every day: it comes for a week, goes for a few days, comes back. Like a relative.
Drenching sweats at night, with a smell he describes as 'wet hay'. His wife describes it differently.
Aching knees and lower back. Malaria tests negative three times, typhoid test negative, and two courses of antibiotics from the chemist did nothing.
His liver and spleen are a little big. He drinks milk warm from his own buffaloes, never boiled. 'Boiling kills the taste, Doctor.'
Two of his buffaloes lost their calves early this year. The vet said something long in English.
mysteries.explain: A fever that waves for weeks, smelly sweats, joint pains, a big liver and spleen, raw milk and buffaloes losing calves: brucellosis. Doxycycline with rifampicin for six weeks. And boil the milk; the taste will survive.

mysteries.title: The pain under the right ribs
mysteries.patient: Mr. Joseph D'Souza, 39, bus driver, Goa
clues: High fever with shivering for ten days, and a dull pain under his right ribs that he blamed on the bus seat.
The pain goes up into his right shoulder, and it hurts to take a deep breath. He drinks most evenings: 'Only feni, Doctor, it's local.'
Pressing between his right lower ribs makes him jump off the bed. His liver edge is tender and big.
He had loose motions with blood and mucus about a month ago, after a wedding lunch. It settled by itself.
Chest X-ray: the right side of his diaphragm is pushed up. The ultrasound shows one big round hole in the liver, full of something brownish.
mysteries.explain: Fever, a tender big liver, pain into the shoulder, a raised right diaphragm, dysentery a month ago and one cavity full of 'anchovy sauce': an amoebic liver abscess. Metronidazole cures most; a big one gets a needle to drain it.

mysteries.title: The shaky student
clues: His handwriting has gone shaky over six months. His coaching teacher thinks it's exam stress. Everyone in Kota is stressed.
His hands tremble more when he holds them out, like a bird flapping. His speech has gone slurred and slow.
He's become moody and cries easily. His parents think it's a girl. There is no girl. There's barely time to eat.
His liver tests are abnormal. His elder cousin died of 'liver failure' at nineteen. Nobody found out why.
Looking closely at his eyes with a torch: a thin golden-brown ring round the edge of each iris.
mysteries.explain: A teenager with a tremor, slurred speech, mood change, liver trouble, a cousin who died young and copper rings in the eyes (Kayser-Fleischer rings): Wilson's disease. Copper builds up in the liver and brain. Treatable for life, and the family must be screened.

mysteries.title: The tan that wasn't the sun
mysteries.patient: Mrs. Kavita Rane, 36, school teacher, Nashik
clues: Tired for months, losing weight without trying, and dizzy every time she stands up. Her BP lying down is 100/64; standing, 78/50.
She craves salt. She eats it straight from the packet. Her husband has stopped buying chips because nothing was left for him.
Her skin has gone darker, most of all in the creases of her palms, her knuckles and old scars. And inside her cheeks.
Sodium 126, potassium 5.9, and a fasting sugar that's low.
She had TB two years ago and stopped the tablets after three months, because she felt better.
mysteries.explain: Tired, thin, low pressure on standing, craving salt, dark creases and gums, low sodium with high potassium, and old half-treated TB in the adrenals: Addison's disease. Steroid replacement for life, and she must never stop it suddenly.

mysteries.title: The spleen from Bihar
mysteries.patient: Mr. Sunil Mahto, 28, mason from Muzaffarpur, working in Pune
clues: Fever on and off for three months, not very high. He kept working because the site pays by the day.
He's lost eight kilos and his belly keeps getting bigger. His friends joke he's pregnant. He's not laughing.
His spleen is huge: it reaches past his belly button. His haemoglobin is 7, and his white cells and platelets are low too.
His skin has gone greyish-dark, especially on his face and hands. In his village, they call it 'the black fever'.
He slept outside on a mud floor at home every summer. Sandflies, he says, are 'just part of the house'.
mysteries.explain: Months of fever, weight loss, a giant spleen, all three blood counts low, darkening skin, Bihar and sandflies: kala-azar. A single dose of liposomal amphotericin B cures most; India has nearly eliminated it, which is exactly why nobody thinks of it in Pune.

mysteries.title: The BP that comes in attacks
mysteries.patient: Mr. Vikram Sethna, 42, chartered accountant, Mumbai
clues: Attacks of pounding headache, sweating and a racing heart, ten to twenty minutes each, a few times a week.
During one attack in the clinic his BP was 220/124. Ten minutes later, 132/84. The panic-attack tablets have done nothing.
The attacks come when he bends to tie his shoes or strains on the toilet. He has lost weight and his fasting sugar is creeping up.
His father had 'BP trouble' young and a 'growth on the neck gland'. His sister had a thyroid operation.
His urine metanephrines are four times the upper limit.
mysteries.explain: Attacks of headache, sweating and palpitations with huge BP spikes that settle in between, set off by pressing on the belly, and a family history of thyroid and neck growths: a phaeochromocytoma, an adrenaline-making tumour (and maybe an inherited syndrome). Alpha-blockers first, then the surgeon. Never a beta-blocker alone.

mysteries.title: The spots on the palms
mysteries.patient: Mrs. Rehana Bibi, 50, from a village in Nadia, West Bengal
clues: Her palms and soles have gone thick, rough and cracked, with hard little corn-like bumps. Creams from the chemist: nothing.
Her chest and back have rain-drop spots: small dark and pale patches all mixed together.
Her feet tingle and burn. She's had a cough for a year, and a sore on her foot that won't heal.
Her neighbours have the same spots. 'The whole lane has it, Doctor. It's the lane.'
The family drinks from the hand pump in the courtyard, sunk into the ground thirty years ago. Their water is clear and tastes fine.
mysteries.explain: Thick rough palms and soles, rain-drop spots, numb feet, a whole lane affected and an old tube well: chronic arsenic poisoning. Clear water can be poisoned water. Safe drinking water is the cure, and watching her skin for cancer.

mysteries.title: The eyelids that give up by evening
mysteries.patient: Ms. Pooja Thakur, 31, call-centre worker, Gurgaon
clues: Her eyelids droop by evening. In the morning she looks fine. Her manager thinks she's sleeping on calls.
She sees double after reading for a while, and it goes away when she rests her eyes.
Her voice goes nasal and weak towards the end of a long shift. Chewing a tough roti tires her jaw halfway through.
An ice pack held on her droopy eyelid for two minutes lifts it noticeably. Her reflexes and sensation are normal.
Her CT chest shows a lump in front of the heart, in the thymus.
mysteries.explain: Weakness that gets worse with use and better with rest, drooping lids and double vision by evening, a tired jaw and voice, a positive ice-pack test and a thymus lump: myasthenia gravis. Pyridostigmine, steroids, and the thymus comes out. Beware: a 'crisis' can stop the breathing.
